passage: I've known Urmila since school, and last month I watched her make the hardest decision I've seen. She had spent two years and most of her savings building a small pottery studio in Bengaluru. It wasn't working. Some weeks nobody came. One evening, over tea, she asked herself out loud, "If I were starting today, knowing what I know, would I open this studio?" She was quiet a long time. Then she said, "No." I thought she'd cry. She did, a little. She said, "I'm sad about the money and the years. But I learned how to run a business, and what customers want." A week later she closed the studio and took a job teaching pottery at a design school. I haven't seen her this light in years. I'm Deepika, and I keep her question on a sticky note now.

qa.q: What did Urmila ask herself over tea?
qa.a: "If I were starting today, knowing what I know, would I open this studio?"

qa.q: How does Deepika seem to feel watching Urmila's decision?
qa.a: Deepika seems moved and admiring, surprised by Urmila's courage and inspired enough to keep her question on a sticky note.

qa.q: What made Urmila's decision wise?
qa.a: She judged from here forward, grieved the cost honestly, took the lessons, and moved on without shame.

qa.q: How did Urmila seem to feel after closing the studio?
qa.a: Urmila seemed lighter and relieved, though still sad about the lost money and years.

grounding: It shows, through a friend's eyes, a woman who asks whether she'd start her studio today, grieves the cost, learns and moves on without shame.

passage:
A Saturday in January. Afreen had spent eight months writing a novel in the evenings after work. Sitting in her Mumbai flat, she read the draft and felt it was dead. She told her friend Nandini, "I can't stop. Eight months!"

A Wednesday two weeks later. Nandini asked, "If you'd never started this novel, would you start it today?" Afreen thought hard. "No. I'd write the short stories I keep thinking about instead." She sat with that. Her eyes filled. "Eight months," she whispered. "That's okay," Nandini said. "You can be sad about it."

A Sunday in March. Afreen had written two short stories. She'd kept three characters from the novel and a lot of what she'd learned about dialogue. She printed the first story and read it aloud to Nandini, smiling. "The novel wasn't wasted," she said. "It taught me."

qa.q: How long had Afreen spent writing the novel?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: How did Afreen feel when she answered Nandini's question?
qa.a: She felt sad, her eyes filling, grieving the eight months, but also clear about what she really wanted.

qa.q: What did Afreen do that made moving on easier?
qa.a: She allowed herself to grieve, kept the lessons and characters from the novel, and started the short stories she actually wanted to write.

qa.q: How does Nandini support Afreen?
qa.a: Nandini asks a clear question and lets Afreen be sad without judging, then celebrates the new stories with her.

grounding: It shows a wise person who asks whether she would start her novel today, grieves the cost, learns from it and moves on, over several weeks.

passage: Uma, you're wondering whether to leave your MBA prep? Let me tell you what I did at twenty-five. I'd spent a year and a lot of money setting up a small tiffin service in Pune with a partner. It was losing money every month. I kept telling myself, just a few more months, or everything is wasted. My mother asked me one evening, "Nikita, beti, if you were starting today, would you open this?" I didn't answer that night. The next morning I wrote it down: No. I cried properly then, for the money and the year. I let myself feel ashamed for one day, and then I stopped. I wrote down what I'd learned: cooking at scale, handling customers, keeping accounts. Then I closed it and joined a food company. I use those lessons every day. That's what Nikita learned: look forward, not back.

qa.q: What did Nikita set up in Pune?
qa.a: A small tiffin service with a partner.

qa.q: How did young Nikita feel once she admitted the answer was no?
qa.a: Nikita cried and felt grief and a day of shame, but then felt clear enough to write down lessons and move on.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Nikita decide?
qa.a: Her mother's question about starting today helped her judge from here forward instead of by the money already spent.

qa.q: How might Nikita's mother have felt asking that question?
qa.a: Her mother probably felt caring and worried, hoping to free her daughter from the stress.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how she asked whether she'd start her business today, grieved the cost, learned from it and moved on without lasting shame.

passage: In their village near Palakkad, Darshan, eight, played marbles with his friend Jomon every evening under the tamarind tree. On Monday, Darshan won Jomon's blue marble. He smiled, put it in his pocket, and forgot about it by dinner. On Tuesday, he lost his own green marble, the one with the gold swirl, to Jomon. He burst into tears. He cried all the way home and wouldn't eat. His mother asked what happened. "Jomon took my green one!" "But you won his blue one yesterday." "That's different!" He hugged his knees on the verandah, sobbing. The blue marble sat forgotten in his pocket. The green one felt like it had been torn from him.

qa.q: What colour was the marble Darshan won on Monday?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: Why did losing the green marble hurt Darshan so much more than winning the blue one pleased him?
qa.a: Losing something he owned felt like it was torn away, so the hurt was much heavier than the small happiness of winning an equal marble.

qa.q: How could Darshan's mother help him feel better?
qa.a: She could let him cry, then gently remind him of the blue marble and suggest he can win the green one back another day.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel about winning the green marble?
qa.a: Jomon might feel pleased at first, then awkward seeing his friend so upset.

grounding: It shows a boy who cries harder over losing a marble than he celebrates winning one, as losing something owned feels heavier.

passage: In Seville, Pablo and his friend Siddiq traded football cards at the school gate every morning. On Monday, Pablo got a card he'd wanted from Siddiq in a trade. He said "cool" and put it in his album. On Wednesday, Siddiq asked for Pablo's goalkeeper card in exchange for an equally good striker. Pablo held the goalkeeper tight. "No way." "But the striker's just as good!" "It's mine." Siddiq finally talked him into it. Pablo handed it over and immediately felt awful. He sulked all day. He didn't even look at the new striker card. That night he asked his mother if he could trade it back. "Why? You got a good card." "But I lost my goalkeeper," he said, near tears.

qa.q: What card did Pablo give up on Wednesday?
qa.a: His goalkeeper card.

qa.q: Why did Pablo feel so bad after an equal trade?
qa.a: Giving up a card he owned felt like a painful loss, heavier than the pleasure of getting an equally good one, so he felt hurt and near tears.

qa.q: What could Pablo think about before trading next time?
qa.a: He could remind himself that losing a card usually feels worse than it is, and decide if the new card is really worth the same.

qa.q: How might Siddiq see Pablo's reaction?
qa.a: Siddiq may feel confused, since he offered an equally good card, and a bit annoyed if Pablo wants to trade back.

grounding: It shows a boy who feels much worse about giving up a card than he feels good about getting an equal one.

passage: In the Class 3 classroom, Francis had a collection of scented erasers. On Thursday, the class played a quiz game where the winner took an eraser from the loser. Francis won a strawberry eraser from Swati. He smiled, said "yes!" and forgot it. Then he lost his mango eraser to another boy. His face crumpled. He cried so hard the teacher came over. "But you won one too," she said kindly. "I don't care about that one! I want my mango!" Swati, whose eraser he had won, leaned over. "Now you know how I felt." Francis wiped his nose, still sniffling. The strawberry eraser lay on his desk, untouched. His mind was only on the one he had lost.

qa.q: What scent was the eraser Francis won from Swati?
qa.a: Strawberry.

qa.q: Why did Francis cry so hard over losing the mango eraser?
qa.a: Losing something he owned felt much heavier than winning an equal one, so he felt deeply hurt while the win barely registered.

qa.q: How could the teacher help Francis with this feeling?
qa.a: She could let him be sad, then talk about how losing often feels bigger than winning, and maybe suggest games without taking things.

qa.q: How might Swati feel when Francis cries?
qa.a: Swati may feel a mix of sympathy and understanding, since she just lost her own eraser.

grounding: It shows a boy who cries harder over losing an eraser than he celebrates winning one, as losing something owned feels heavier.

passage: In the small-town school in Sangli, the debate club was starting, and Chetan's classmate Nikita asked him to join. He was good at speaking; everyone said so. But he was also first in class, and the debate club met on Fridays, when he usually revised. "What if my rank drops?" he said. "And what if I'm bad at debate and people laugh?" Nikita shrugged. "What if you're great?" Chetan didn't answer. He kept revising on Fridays. He also stopped sitting with his old friends at lunch, because a new group had invited him, and he didn't want to lose either. So he ate alone, reading. By December, his rank was still first. But he felt oddly small. The debate club won the district trophy. He watched from the back of the hall, clapping, alone.

qa.a: On Fridays.

qa.q: Why did Chetan refuse to join the debate club?
qa.a: He feared losing his first rank or being laughed at more than he valued possible gains, so staying safe felt better even though it left him feeling small.

qa.a: He could have tried a few debate sessions while keeping some Friday revision, testing whether his rank really drops.

grounding: It shows a teenager who avoids a new club and friend group because losing his current standing feels worse than any possible gain.

passage: In Lagos, Chidi was the fastest runner in his year. His friend Oskar, whose family had moved from Norway, invited him to join the new chess club after school. Chidi was curious. He liked puzzles. But the chess club met at the same time as athletics training. What if he fell behind in running? What if he lost at chess and people saw? He told Oskar, "Maybe next term." Next term, he said the same. Oskar made new friends in the club; they laughed together at lunch. Chidi kept winning races. But when he passed the chess room, he felt a pang. He had kept everything he had. He just hadn't gained anything new. His world, he thought, felt a bit smaller than before.

qa.q: What was Chidi known for in his year?
qa.a: He was the fastest runner in his year.

qa.q: Why did Chidi keep saying 'maybe next term'?
qa.a: The fear of losing his running edge or looking bad at chess felt bigger than the chance of enjoying something new, so safe felt better, though he later felt a pang.

qa.q: What could Chidi do to try chess without much risk?
qa.a: He could ask to join the chess club on a day without athletics, or try one session to see how it feels.

qa.q: How might Oskar see Chidi's repeated 'maybe next term'?
qa.a: Oskar may feel a bit disappointed but moves on, making new friends in the club.

grounding: It shows a teenager who avoids joining a new club because losing his current standing feels worse than any possible gain, so his world shrinks.
